catalog_quote: 2.7 Word stress. In basic roots, primary stress is normally applied to the penultimate syllable of a word. Secondary stress applies to every alternate syllable to the left of the penultimate syllable: /ˈga.ni/ 'eat', /βa.ˈtsu.ru/ 'choose', /ˌma.ri.ˈbu.ku/ 'humpback snapper'. Abma is quantity-sensitive. Long vowels take stress, regardless of their position in the word: /ˈβa:.ta/ 'be tight', /ˈe:.naŋ/ 'something, someone', /mwa.ˈte:.te/ 'chicken', /ta.ˈka:/ 'god'. Words ending in closed syllables typically receive word-final stress: /lel.ˈkat/ 'be angry', /sa.ˈdok/ 'sit down', /ha.ˈβin/ 'woman', /me.ˈram/ 'moonlight', /le.ˈleh/ 'bathe', /na.ˈŋih/ 'when'. Where long vowels and closed final syllables both occur in a single word, then long vowels take precedence for the purposes of stress assignment: /ˈha:.pak/ 'child', /ˈtsu:.buŋ/ 'morning', /ˈne:.bik/ 'do.IRR'. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: default penult, long vowel stressed anywhere, final closed syllable attracts stress, CVV > final CVC; secondaries alternate leftward; author hedges beyond the root) rests on the standard and only reference grammar of Abma (Schneider 2010, PL 608, from her 2006 PhD), which we hold as the ANU open text layer; the deciding quotation is present verbatim at §2.7 p.35 and the supporting passages (§3.1.2.2 p.45, fn.11, §2.8, §2.9) are all present as cited. The hedged quantity-sensitive coding faithfully reflects the author's own caveats ('typically', 'not straightforward', 'merits a study of its own'). Glottolog lists no phonology work; the one open item not yet obtained (Schneider & Gray 2015) was downloaded and is silent on stress; Gray's archived web page is silent; no instrumental or theoretical stress study of Apma surfaced. Nothing found suggests a reclassify.
